The stock market heads into another critical week with earnings season moving into a higher gear, putting some of Wall Street's biggest names back in the spotlight.

TSLA, SPCX Earnings Put Musk's AI, Robotaxi Bets Under The Microscope

Tesla Inc. (TSLA) and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) will give investors a rare back-to-back look at Elon Musk's sprawling AI ambitions, with SpaceX reporting Tuesday and Tesla following Wednesday.

For SpaceX, the focus will extend well beyond its traditional rocket business as investors assess the growth of Starlink and its emerging AI operations.

Tesla, meanwhile, enters its report with third-quarter deliveries already in hand, shifting attention toward margins, cash flow and how aggressively the company plans to fund its robotaxi, Optimus and AI push.

Investors will also keep an eye out for potential management commentary on the speculated merger of the two companies led by Musk.

Wall Street expects Tesla to report earnings per share (EPS) of $0.45 on revenue of $28.11 billion, according to Fiscal.ai data. SpaceX is expected to report an EPS of $0.18 on revenue of $13.16 billion.

META Kicks Off Hyperscaler Earnings As WDC Tests The AI Memory Trade

Meta Platforms Inc. (META) is set to kick off the next major stretch of hyperscaler earnings on Wednesday, putting the spotlight squarely on the economics of the AI spending boom.

Investors will be looking for updates regarding Meta's massive investments in data centers and AI infrastructure, and whether they are beginning to translate into stronger growth and returns.

Meta is expected to report an EPS of $6.76 on revenue of $63.39 billion, after the bell.

Joining Meta will be Western Digital Corp. (WDC), which is expected to report an EPS of $4.08 on revenue of $4.13 billion.

Here's a head-scratcher: iShares Core Dividend (DIVB), a dividend-focused exchange-traded fund (ETF) that we recently added to the Kiplinger ETF 20, gained 36% over the past 12 months through August, handily beating the 20% return in the S&P 500 over the same period. (Since June 30, when we added the ETF to the Kip ETF 20 roster, the fund has climbed nearly 12%, well ahead of the S&P 500, which has risen 3%.)

The index fund targets stocks in U.S. companies that pay the fattest dividends and buy back the biggest number of shares by dollar value. It holds roughly 380 stocks and yields 2.9%.

At last report, the fund's top holdings — International Business Machines (IBM), Automated Data Processing (ADP), Accenture (ACN) and Paychex (PAYX) — bore no resemblance to the top stocks in the S&P 500: Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon.com (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOGL). That's a plus in our view.

That said, tech shares, such as Cisco Systems (CSCO) and Dell Technologies (DELL), played a role in the fund's superior performance earlier this year. (The fund reconstitutes every June, and those stocks are no longer in the portfolio.)

Energy stocks, boosted by higher oil prices amid tension in the Middle East, helped too. Top-10 stock Exxon Mobil (XOM) has climbed 26% since the start of the year.

A leader among peers

Core Dividend's long-term record sparkles as well. The ETF's annualized return over the past five years, 14%, ranks among the top 7% of its peer group (funds that focus on large-company stocks trading at bargain prices), and it beats the gain in the S&P 500.

The portfolio skews more toward growth-oriented sectors than its peer ETFs do. According to financial data firm Morningstar, tech stocks make up 33% of the portfolio, nearly double the exposure to that sector in the typical large-value fund.

But Core Dividend also holds a chunk of assets in sectors that tilt toward value, such as energy, financial services and healthcare.

Fresh projects in quantum computing and semiconductor research, including IBM's work on nanostack transistors and fault tolerant quantum systems, may support expectations for future cash generation but can also shape when those cash flows arrive and how much investment is required to get there.

Does International Business Machines Look Undervalued on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here takes IBM's future cash generation and discounts it back to today. On that view, International Business Machines is being valued on free cash flow that was about $13.1b over the last twelve months, with the model assuming that this gradually grows rather than shrinking away. The projections build in a moderate step up in annual cash available to shareholders over the coming decade, not a sharp spike or collapse.

The DCF outcome sits meaningfully above the current share price of $232.14, which means the market is not paying for all of those projected dollars of cash yet. IBM's push into nanostack 3D transistor architecture with Siemens gives some context, because heavier near term investment and technical risk can keep investors cautious even when long term cash estimates are higher. title: IBM spent $11 billion on growth as its own software stalls
detail:
IBM spent $11 billion on growth as its own software stalls
Opeyemi Babalola, Aparajita Chatterjee
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 9:33 AM MST 6 min read
IBM
Trade IBM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) finished buying real-time data company Confluent in March, and the deal is doing its job of adding software growth. The trouble is that it now adds nearly all of it.

Strip out acquisitions, and IBM's own software sales were flat last quarter. Chief Financial Officer Jim Kavanaugh told analysts as much on IBM's earnings call on Wednesday, July 22, 2026.

IBM's software unit brought in $7.76 billion in the second quarter, up 5%, according to its earnings release. That is about 45% of IBM's revenue for the quarter, so its growth sets the tone for the stock.

Confluent explains most of that gain. IBM closed the deal, which valued Confluent at about $11 billion, on Tuesday, March 17, 2026, according to IBM's announcement.

IBM's leadership says the weak spot is narrow. "Our second quarter software shortfall was limited to a capex-sensitive area of the portfolio," CEO Arvind Krishna said on the call. That means big, one-time licenses paid from equipment budgets, much of it tied to IBM's mainframes.

Krishna told Fox Business in July that a third of the deals that slipped had already come back. Even so, IBM is leaning on a purchase while it waits for its homegrown business to restart.

Bank of America thinks the wait is worth it. According to the BofA note shared with TheStreet, analyst Wamsi Mohan kept his Buy rating and $280 price target on Thursday, October 15, 2026.

Also read: After a brutal slide, IBM sells smaller firms an 'AI-ready' core

The report's title is blunt: "Modestly better 3Q but 4Q has to carry the year." Mohan's team calls IBM's organic software growth, which excludes acquisitions, "improving but below ideal."

Confluent is carrying IBM's software growth

BofA estimates IBM's own software sales will slip about 0.3% in the third quarter, a drop of roughly $23 million. An estimated $350 million from Confluent should still lift total software growth to about 3.5%, according to the note.

That cushion has an expiration date. Acquired sales count as new growth only for the first year, so Confluent's lift disappears in the second quarter of 2027.

IBM's own software sales were flat last quarter, leaving its $11 billion Confluent deal to carry growth.SOPA Images / Getty Images
The mainframe slump is a drag IBM can't buy away

The soft spot is the mainframe, the heavy-duty computer IBM says runs the world's most critical business transactions. IBM Z revenue fell 42% in the second quarter, according to the earnings release.

IBM expected a dip as it lapped last year's z17 launch, Krishna wrote in a letter to investors. It did not expect clients to shift so much spending to servers, storage and memory ahead of expected price increases.

Why You Should Think About Palantir Differently Now

Image from Pixabay

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock trades at 78.2 times sales, compared to 3.1 for the S&P 500. Investors paying that premium need to know exactly what they are buying, and the case Palantir makes has evolved. During the fiscal Q3 2024 earnings call, executives highlighted the fast-growing number of U.S. businesses signing on as customers. By the latest call in fiscal Q2 2026, the focus had shifted. So what does management talk up now?

Palantir Now Makes The Case For Sovereign AI

By sovereign AI, Palantir means an architecture where companies maintain full control over their own data and the artificial intelligence built upon it. During the fiscal Q2 2026 call, held August 3, 2026, executives reported immense demand from enterprises for this capability. They contrasted this approach with purchasing external services from AI labs, a process they described as paying outside vendors to move proprietary corporate knowledge into third-party models.

The pitch sounded quite different during the fiscal Q3 2024 call. At that time, leadership highlighted that Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count grew to 321. Expanding that baseline served as a clear signal that more U.S. companies were adopting the software.

While Palantir still reports the customer count, the metric no longer takes center stage. Instead, the company links sovereign AI directly to increased spending per client. Customers that previously utilized only the Foundry software now want access to the broader sovereign AI stack. The core argument now rests on the size of individual customer commitments, rather than the sheer number of clients.

Shifts like this test every retirement plan. If your advisor recently retired, it is a good moment for a free second opinion from our partner firm.

Palantir's Business Customers Are Spending Much Larger Sums

Sales to the U.S. businesses are growing much faster than the number of businesses buying. Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count reached 653 in fiscal Q2 2026, up 35% from a year earlier. Over that same period, U.S. commercial revenue rose 149% to $764 million. These buyers belong to Palantir's commercial segment, a division that generated $2.07 billion in fiscal 2025, accounting for 46.3% of the company's total revenue that year.

Contract values follow a similar trajectory. U.S. businesses signed deals with Palantir worth $2.132 billion in total in fiscal Q2 2026, up 153% from a year earlier. Consequently, the average customer is committing significantly more capital than they were just a year ago. Executives labeled that contract total a record, forming the foundation of the case they now present.

title: Why Did Accenture Stock Jump?
detail:
Why Did Accenture Stock Jump?
Trefis Team
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 7:02 PM MST 3 min read
ACN
^GSPC
IBM
CTSH
BAH
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Between July 17 and October 15, 2026, Accenture (ACN) stock rose 57.9%, while the S&P 500 gained 4.1%. The single biggest day in that run occurred on October 1. The company reported its fiscal fourth quarter results, provided a forecast for fiscal 2027, and saw its shares rise 15.8%. So did Accenture's business change as much as its share price did?

Investors Now Pay Far More For Accenture's Profit

Not nearly as much. For fiscal 2026, which ended August 31, Accenture earned $13.56 a share, up 12% from $12.15 a year earlier. Part of that gain came from smaller one-time charges: business optimization costs reduced earnings by $0.78 a share in fiscal 2025 but only $0.41 in fiscal 2026. Excluding those costs, earnings rose 8% to $13.97 a share. In the fourth quarter alone, earnings rose 9% to $3.29 a share against an adjusted $3.03 a year earlier. That is steady growth, but the share price rose about five times as fast. Investors now pay far more for that profit. At the end of June, the shares traded at 10.0 times trailing earnings, the lowest at any quarter end since fiscal 2016, when this record begins. The share price had already risen 16.8% from its June 30 close by July 17, when this run began. On October 15 the shares traded at 16.6 times trailing earnings, still below the S&P 500 at 22.7 times.

Accenture did not rise alone. Over those same dates, peer Cognizant gained 48%. On October 1, Reuters reported that Accenture's forecast of stronger-than-expected annual revenue growth had eased concerns that AI-driven disruption could weigh on technology spending.

Accenture's Bookings Ran Ahead Of Revenue

The October report showed clients are still signing new work with Accenture. Revenue for the fiscal fourth quarter reached $18.7 billion. That figure was up 7% in local currency, coming in above the top of the range management had forecast. Meanwhile, new bookings, the value of contracts signed in the quarter, were $22.2 billion, or 1.2 times revenue. Managed services bookings reached a record $12.8 billion, a category management says comes from large deals that are lumpy.

Some of that work involves AI. Nearly 100 more clients began their first advanced AI work with Accenture in the quarter, bringing the fiscal 2026 total to more than 400. Asked about AI lowering the value of renewed contracts, management said the company is giving clients more productivity from AI and offsetting that with new kinds of work and more scope. Not everything improved, though. Management also noted that Accenture saw lower pricing in many areas of its business in the fourth quarter.

International Business Machines Corporation IBM is scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 earnings after the closing bell on Oct. 21. In the quarter, the company is likely to have recorded marginally higher revenues from the Consulting segment driven by rising demand for technology consulting and business transformation services.

Factors at Play

The Consulting segment comprises Strategy and Technology (previously reported as Business Transformation and Technology Consulting) and Intelligent Operations (previously reported as Application Operations). It provides consulting and application management services that offer value and innovation to clients by leveraging industry, technology and business strategy and process know-how.

During the to-be-reported quarter, IBM partnered with India-based artificial intelligence (AI) company Sarvam to develop and test sovereign AI technologies for government agencies and regulated industries in the subcontinent. The collaboration aims to build AI systems that give organizations greater control over data, governance and operations while supporting digital transformation across the public sector. IBM also collaborated with Arm Holdings plc to give enterprises more software choices for mission-critical workloads. IBM's latest processor will enable Arm-native Linux environments to run alongside z/OS and Linux on IBM Z, giving enterprises access to a broader software ecosystem while maintaining security, reliability and scalability. These are likely to have generated additional revenues for the Consulting segment.

In the third quarter, IBM acquired Logiq Consulting, a U.K.-based cybersecurity consultancy, to strengthen its secure digital transformation capabilities and expand its presence across highly regulated industries. The acquisition reinforces IBM's strategy of expanding its cybersecurity portfolio while capitalizing on the growing demand for secure hybrid cloud and AI solutions.

Logiq Consulting brings specialized Secure by Design capabilities, allowing organizations to integrate cybersecurity throughout the technology lifecycle rather than addressing vulnerabilities after deployment. These capabilities complement IBM's existing cybersecurity transformation services and SiXworks' digital transformation expertise in defense and public sector markets. In addition, Logiq's DISX managed sovereign collaboration platform enables government suppliers to exchange sensitive information securely with U.K. government and defense organizations while maintaining control over data management. Integrating these capabilities with IBM's hybrid cloud, AI and consulting expertise could create opportunities for cross-selling services and expanding relationships with security-conscious customers. The buyout also boosts IBM's digital sovereignty offerings as governments and regulated enterprises increasingly prioritize data control, regulatory compliance and operational resilience.

Factors at Play

The Software segment includes Hybrid Cloud, Automation and Data and Transaction Processing.

During the third quarter, IBM entered into a multi-year, $240 million agreement with Together AI to support the growing demand for enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) inference. The partnership will enable IBM to expand its cloud infrastructure offerings for open-source AI workloads and strengthen its position in the rapidly growing AI infrastructure market. Under the agreement, the company plans to deploy a large cluster of NVIDIA's HGX B300 systems on IBM Cloud and provide Together AI with enterprise-grade cloud infrastructure powered by NVIDIA's advanced computing and Spectrum-X Ethernet networking technologies.

The deployment is designed to support high-performance AI inference and make large-scale workloads more cost-effective. The collaboration also expands IBM's broader relationship with NVIDIA across AI infrastructure and software. The companies are advancing solutions in GPU-accelerated data analytics, unstructured data processing, hybrid cloud infrastructure and consulting services. These capabilities are expected to help enterprises deploy AI workloads across cloud and on-premises environments with greater performance, flexibility and scalability.

IBM also introduced a new set of AI-powered experiences for the 2026 U.S. Open to make live tennis more personalized, informative and interactive for millions of fans worldwide. By turning complex court-level data into accessible insights, the company helped fans better understand the game through advanced technology. Such investments in innovation and collaborations will likely boost IBM's commercial prospects and are likely to have generated incremental revenues for the Software segment.

In the to-be-reported quarter, IBM collaborated with LTM to strengthen enterprise software supply chain security through AI-driven vulnerability remediation. The partnership aims to help enterprises identify and address vulnerabilities in open-source software while minimizing disruptions to business-critical applications. Per the collaboration, LTM will leverage Lightwell's AI-powered remediation capabilities to help enterprises implement validated software fixes at scale. Building on its long-standing relationship as an IBM Platinum Partner, LTM plans to offer services spanning dependency analysis, risk-based prioritization, DevSecOps integration, testing, validation and large-scale deployment support. The initiative combines Lightwell's software remediation capabilities with LTM's expertise in application modernization, cybersecurity and cloud technologies. The deal is expected to strengthen IBM's position in the enterprise software security market as organizations increasingly prioritize cybersecurity and software supply chain resilience.

So how did people who bought HPE's earlier falls do?

HPE Stock Was Higher A Year After Past Falls

Realizing those gains required patience. In the median case, the stock's lowest close in the following year was 8.6% below its close on the day of the initial fall. Is HPE Still Turning Orders Into Sales?

The company is doing just that, though not as fast as customers are ordering. Revenue grew 33.7% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026, which ended July 31, while operating profit expanded even faster. Part of the revenue growth came from HPE's acquisition of Juniper Networks. On management's figures, which count Juniper in both years, networking revenue grew 10%. The operating margin reached 12.0%, compared to 4.7% in the same quarter a year earlier. Cash from operations accounted for 13.4% of revenue, standing close to the 13.2% recorded the previous quarter.

title: Accenture's $8B Acquisition Push: A Growth Catalyst for ACN Stock?
detail:
Accenture's $8B Acquisition Push: A Growth Catalyst for ACN Stock?
Shuvra Shankar Dey

Accenture plc ACN is stepping up its acquisition strategy, with approximately $8 billion in planned investments for fiscal 2027. The aggressive spending underscores its efforts to strengthen industry expertise, expand into emerging markets and accelerate growth. However, integration challenges could complicate the company's expansion ambitions.

ACN's $8B Acquisition Pipeline

Accenture invested $4.9 billion across 17 acquisitions in fiscal 2026 compared with $1.5 billion across 23 transactions in fiscal 2025. The substantial increase in spending despite fewer transactions highlights its growing appetite for larger acquisitions.

For fiscal 2027, approximately $3 billion of the projected $8 billion relates to Cyber Operational Technology (OT) acquisitions, including Dragos. These transactions shifted from the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 to the first quarter of fiscal 2027 due to regulatory timing.

Management expects to deploy another approximately $5 billion toward acquisitions during fiscal 2027.

Accenture's Inorganic Growth Expectations

Accenture's inorganic contribution to growth was approximately 1.5 percentage points in fiscal 2026, down from 3 percentage points in fiscal 2025.

For fiscal 2027, management anticipates inorganic growth of about 2-2.5 percentage points, highlighting the potential benefits of its expanding acquisition portfolio.

The strategy centers on scaling high-growth businesses, strengthening industry-specific capabilities and entering new growth markets. Cybersecurity-related investments could further enhance its enterprise technology offerings.

What Could Limit ACN's Acquisition Upside?

Despite promising opportunities, substantial acquisition spending carries integration and execution risks. Delays in closing transactions, higher integration costs and weaker-than-expected synergies could weigh on returns.

Accenture's ability to convert its expanding portfolio into sustained revenue growth and stronger profitability will ultimately determine whether its acquisition strategy translates into meaningful shareholder value.

How Do IBM and Cognizant Compare?

International Business Machines Corporation IBM and Cognizant Technology Solutions Corporation CTSH are two U.S.-listed competitors pursuing growth through technology investments and acquisitions.

IBM continues to strengthen its hybrid cloud, artificial intelligence, and consulting capabilities through strategic transactions. These investments help IBM address evolving enterprise technology requirements, although integration complexities and competitive pressures remain concerns. IBM's diversified portfolio provides additional growth opportunities.
